articles.title_orig: In Choosing Shenzhen for Trump-Putin Summit, Xi Shows Off His Tech Ambitions
articles.title_zh: In Choosing Shenzhen for Trump-Putin Summit, Xi Shows Off His Tech Ambitions
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

The Russian Embassy in the Netherlands on Wednesday posted a statement asking if the Netherlands had openly joined the conflict in Ukraine on Kyiv's side after a Dutch-based company said its missiles had been used by Ukraine in an attack on the Crimean Bridge.
Ukrainian drones and missiles destroyed the central road section of the bridge linking Russia and Crimea on Tuesday, inflicting a military and symbolic blow on President Vladimir Putin days before he is due to meet the leaders of China and the U.S.
Destinus, a Dutch-headquartered startup, said Tuesday that its missiles were the only foreign-made weapons used in the Ukrainian attack on the Crimean Bridge, a rare operational role for a Western manufacturer in one of Kyiv's most significant long-range strikes of the war.
"Moscow has been duly informed of the NL (Netherlands) involvement," the Russian embassy said in a statement on X above a statement from Destinus detailing its role in the bridge attack.
"The confession has been well noted. Is The Hague openly joining the conflict?," the embassy said.

articles.title_orig: Iran widens Gulf attacks, targeting US air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain
articles.title_zh: Iran widens Gulf attacks, targeting US air base in Kuwait and sites in Bahrain
articles.content_orig:
Iran said its army targeted U.S. drone and missile installations at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem air base, according to local media , extending a series of attacks on Gulf states hosting American forces.
Kuwait's army said on Tuesday evening that its air defenses had countered hostile drone attacks, without providing further details.
Tensions between Iran and the U.S. have escalated sharply in recent days as strikes resumed across the Middle East, even as diplomatic talks continued.
Bahrain has also sustained a wave of Iranian drone strikes , issuing an "all-clear" alert on Wednesday after its air defenses intercepted several aerial threats. Iran has previously claimed attacks on U.S. radar systems in Bahrain.
CNN reported late Monday that U.S. intelligence found Iran was developing plans that could involve a so-called dirty bomb to target Washington, D.C. The administration officials, including President Donald Trump, have played down any imminent threat while saying the government continues to monitor the situation.
Speaking at the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila, Philippines, Trump warned that Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid before" if such a plan existed.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio echoed Trump's comments when addressing reporters in Manila, saying he did not see any imminent threats to the U.S. capital, but that the government is "always on the lookout for anything that's a threat."
Trump nodded and said, "We are looking into it," while adding, "We are doing very well in Iran."
The renewed attacks come as diplomatic efforts to end the U.S.-Israel war with Iran, now in its ninth month, appear to be stalled, while disruptions continue to weigh on energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Crude futures settled lower amid signs of recovering oil flows through the critical waterway. The International Energy Agency said Friday that the global oil supply had surpassed demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war and projected the market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter.
The U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 1.2% to $84.9 a barrel, while Brent was down 0.48% at $92.7 per barrel.

articles.title_zh: Grand Theft Auto VI Uses AMD FSR 4 On Xbox Series S, Upscaling 720p To 1080p While Still Running Ray Traced Global Illumination
articles.content_orig:
During Grand Theft Auto VI 's review period , Rockstar Games offered us the chance to send some questions to the developers. Being a tech-focused website, there was a lot we wanted to know about the studio's design goals for this iteration of the RAGE engine .
Did they try to achieve a frame rate higher than 30 frames per second ? What were the rendering resolutions for each system? What kind of challenges did adding ray traced global illumination present, and what was their approach to HDR support?
All of these questions are answered below in a lengthy statement crafted by Jonathon Ashcroft - Senior Vice President of Technology, Chris Oat – Technical Director: Engine and Graphics, and Marc Chambers – Technology Production Director.
It became clear early on that given the scale of the team’s ambition, we’d be targeting 30fps on this generation of hardware. We’ve put a lot of effort into balancing presentation, simulation, and gameplay, as well as ensuring the input latency is vastly improved vs. Grand Theft Auto V and Red Dead Redemption 2. Part of that process was determining our base resolution and upscaling solution. We evaluated a variety of approaches for each console, then selected a combination of each that gave us the look and performance we needed.
On all platforms, the picture is then composited with a 4K UI and presented. For each console, we’ve arrived at our solution through careful evaluation of both the visuals and the performance.  We built our core lighting, frame processing, and final presentation pipeline with both HDR and SDR support in mind from the outset. We calibrated our engine’s in-game light sources according to the real-world physical properties of natural and artificial light sources.
We also built a new physically-based material library used to represent every material type you will see in game. From the way muddy alligator skin glistens in the Leonida sunshine, to the way hair and clothing reacts to the dynamic light shows in a nightclub, and the complex lighting interactions of exotic vehicle paint zipping under highway street lights — it was all built to behave according the physical laws of light. Finally, that rendered frame goes through an imaging pipeline modelled after real word cinematic camera and film treatment, much like you would expect of a modern movie. The aim is always to try and create and preserve emersion for the player, so they can experience it as the team imagined it, whether they are experiencing the game in HDR or SDR.
This focus on lighting made it vital for us to ensure we could use the same lighting solution on each console, including the Xbox Series S, where memory pressure posed a bit of a challenge. The results made that a challenge worth overcoming. There are indeed some differences between the implementations per console, as we rebalance the RTGI features to achieve the best presentation based on each platform’s capabilities. As with everything, we tune on a given piece of hardware to achieve the presentation we’re looking for, so there’s no single solution.
I also asked Rockstar a couple of more artistic questions, which were answered separately by the studio's VP of Art, Michael Kane . You can find them below.
The game's corners of the screen often seem a little darkened, kind of like a vignette effect. Can you confirm that's the case? If so, would it be possible to add it as a toggle option for those who dislike it?
Michael Kane, Vice President of Dynamic Art: The vignette effect is an artistic choice. We currently do not support any toggle, but we have recently identified and fixed an issue where it was becoming stronger than intended in certain circumstances.
In key Grand Theft Auto VI artworks, Jason looks very different from the in-game character, whereas Lucia looks much closer. How did your design for each character evolve through development, and did you have any specific references or inspirations that you can share?
Michael Kane, Vice President of Dynamic Art: There could typically be a perceptual interpretation of the key art versus in-game, especially for Jason… because both of them are so customizable, we think many players will maybe want ‘their Jason’ to have a mustache or long hair in a certain style or colour etc when they play. So far, we’ve only seen those more diverse looks on him in screenshots and not key marketing art, so that’s the best anchor point for our intention for him – that’s his ground truth, in-game.
About the author : With over two decades of experience in gaming journalism, Alessio Palumbo has led the gaming vertical at Wccftech since August 2015. He started working at a young age for Italian websites like Everyeye.it, Gamestar.it, Nextgame.it, and Multiplayer.it before kickstarting the indie English-language publication Worlds Factory as its founder and Editor in Chief. 

In the last decade, he has coordinated the overall output of Wccftech's gaming section, managed PR relations, assigned reviews, produced daily news coverage, edited gaming content as needed, and delivered game reviews.  

Arguably, his trademark content is the long series of exclusive developer interviews that have been cited by Wikipedia and by the biggest news media and gaming publications. 

His passion for technology also makes him knowledgeable when it comes to gaming hardware and tech. His favorite genres include RPGs, MMORPGs, and action/adventure games.
Follow Wccftech on Google to get more of our news coverage in your feeds.

articles.title_orig: Stock futures rise as Nvidia gains on earnings beat and solid outlook: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures rise as Nvidia gains on earnings beat and solid outlook: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures climbed Wednesday morning after the S&P 500 fell for a fourth straight day. Traders also weighed Nvidia 's better-than-expected earnings report.
Nasdaq-100 futures were up 1%, while S&P 500 futures added 0.58%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 0.32%.
Shares of Nvidia were almost 3% higher in premarket trade, after jumping 4% in extended trading after the company's profit and revenue in the third quarter beat analysts' estimates. The company also lifted its revenue guidance for the fiscal year ending January 2028, calling for 75% growth year over year.
"The fact that they gave guidance is huge," said Gene Munster, managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, on CNBC's "Closing Bell: Overtime. " " That is a very bullish sign. I expect the stock to move higher based just on that alone."
Neocloud companies also rose in extended trading. CoreWeave advanced 8%, while Nebius Group gained 10%.
During the regular trading day, the Dow dropped 1.6%. The S&P 500 slipped 1% and notched its lowest closing level since July 29, while the Nasdaq Composite shed 0.7%. During the day, the tech-heavy index touched its lowest level since April.
Looking ahead, traders are awaiting building permits and housing starts data. The Federal Open Market Committee's minutes from its October meeting will also be out in the afternoon. Federal Reserve policymakers last month decided to keep the overnight funds rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%.
On the earnings front, Lowe's, Target and TJ Maxx-parent TJX Cos are slated to report Wednesday morning.
Later this week, investors are awaiting a blockbuster initial public offering from Anthropic. The AI giant's shares are expected to be priced above the current range between $70 and $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
Across the Atlantic, stock markets were mixed on Wednesday, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 hovering just below the flatline in morning trade. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 was 0.34% down, with France's CAC 40 sliding almost 0.1%, but Germany's DAX advanced 0.15%.
Most Asian markets closed in positive territory after a choppy trading session. South Korea's Kospi led gains in the region as chip heavyweights gained ground, ending 1.99% higher at 5,067.44, while Japan's Nikkei 225 gained 0.28% to close at 59,024.28,
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 0.87% lower in its final hour of trade, while the CSI 300 on mainland China advanced 0.18% to 3,983.77. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 slipped 0.69%, marking a fifth straight day of losses.
Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at New Jersey-based Questar Capital Partners, said in a note Wednesday that Nvidia is "uninvestable."
"Nvidia is the Jenga tower of the whole AI trade, and that is not a compliment," he said. "A week ago, we thought this was a pedestrian story about a CEO whose ego got the best of him. Then we found out there was no clear succession plan, and poor corporate governance, with no Chairman until this scandal came to light."
He added that Nvidia's delayed 10-Q was a "red flag, as it's out of character from its previous releases."
"We believe there are significant questions about where Nvidia has been selling its chips," Reyle said. "For investors who own the stock, this is an immediate sell in our view. We have never owned Nvidia and believe the stock has been and remains uninvestable."
Shares of Nvidia were up around 4% in pre-market trading on Wednesday.
"There's another company set to begin a spectacular run (Anthropic), and every moment spent worrying about Nvidia is time that could have been spent finding the next winner," Reyle added. "News flash: NVDA ain't it."
Nvidia stock was up nearly 4% in premarket trading on Wednesday after reporting another earnings beat , as the fallout from CEO Jensen Huang's resignation continues to unfold.
The chip giant's stock was 3.96% higher at 5.08 a.m. ET on Wednesday in pre-market trading.
Neoclouds were buoyed by the results. CoreWeave was up 6.2%, Nebius 8.1% and Iren 7.4%.
U.S.-listed semiconductor stocks rose in pre-market trading Wednesday, following Nvidia's earnings beat.
Ahead of the opening bell, Nvidia stock was trading 3.9% higher, with the iShares and VanEck semiconductor ETFs both adding around 2.8%.
Marvell Technology added 4.3%, Arm was up by 3.8% and Micron gained 3.6%. KLA Corporation and AMD also traded more than 3% higher.
President Donald Trump has landed in China for the APEC summit, where he is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the first trilateral talks between the three leaders on Thursday.
The meeting — taking place in Shenzhen, a major tech hub — puts trade and technology in sharp focus. Markets will be watching for any sign of progress on U.S.-China trade tensions or restrictions on advanced AI chips.
Xi opened the summit by calling for fewer trade and investment barriers and closer cooperation on artificial intelligence.
Traders are also watching for any signal on Ukraine, sanctions and energy, and the conflict in the Middle East , which could shape expectations for Russian oil exports and the geopolitical risk premium.
Precious metals sold off Wednesday morning, with gold falling to its lowest level in over a year and silver also plunging to a 52-week low, as expectations of interest rate rises from the Federal Reserve next month drew investors away from non-interest bearing assets.
Gold futures fell 2.34% to $3,761.84, while spot gold was down 2.38% at $3,758%. Silver futures slipped 3.5% to $45.72, as spot silver shed 3.6% to reach $45.67.
Nannette Hechler-Fayd'herbe, Lombard Odier Group's chief investment officer for EMEA and head of investment strategy, sustainability and research, said she remained optimistic on gold over the next 12 months, but warned that investors may need to be patient.
Hechler-Fayd'herbe does not expect the Federal Reserve or other central banks to embark on a sustained series of interest-rate hikes. But with U.S. real yields moving back up to 2.9%, from 2.6% not long ago, conditions are not yet supportive of an immediate rally, she said.
"This of course is not an environment where gold can immediately perform, so a little bit of patience on gold I think is warranted," she told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" Wednesday.
European stock markets were largely negative in early trading on Wednesday, with the Stoxx 600 edging just below the flatline shortly after 8:00 a.m. in London (3:00 a.m. E.T.).
Technology stocks advanced 1.16%, leading continental sectors, while industrial goods added 0.19%. But most other sectors were in the red, with basic resources tumbling 2.41%, while autos fell 0.43%.
Germany's DAX was up almost 0.1% in early trading in Frankfurt.
The U.K.'s FTSE 100 was down 0.32% in London, while in Paris, the CAC 40 was flat.  In Milan, the Italian FTSE MIB was hovering just below the flatline.
Indonesia's central bank on Wednesday raised rates by 25 basis points in a surprise move, bringing its policy rate to 6% — last seen in December 2024.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected the bank to keep rates steady at 5.75%.
The Bank of Indonesia said the move was to strengthen the currency and a preemptive measure to keep inflation in its target range of 1.5% to 3.5%.
The Indonesian rupiah depreciated to a record low of 18,285 against the greenback on Tuesday, while the inflation rate in the country was at 3.23% in October.
Markets in Asia ended mostly higher on Wednesday in choppy trading as investors assessed Nvidia earnings, Japan exports data, and comments from global leaders at the APEC summit in China.
South Korea's Kospi led gains in the region as chip heavyweights rose, rising 2% to 5,067.44. The small-cap Kosdaq also advanced 2% to close at 662.81.
Japan's Nikkei 225 gained 0.28% to close at 59,024.28, while the broad-broad Topix lost 0.42% to 3,824.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 0.87% lower in its final hour of trade, while the CSI 300 on mainland China advanced 0.18% to 3,983

articles.title_zh: Trump heads to China after announcing 'very big trade deal' in Manila
articles.content_orig:
President Trump said on Wednesday the United States had concluded a “very big trade deal” with the Philippines, but offered no details, while Manila said the two countries had reached only an understanding on economic cooperation.
“We’ve just consummated a very big trade deal, the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made so far, and it is a fair deal for both countries,” Trump told a state lunch event at the Philippine presidential palace.
“We were very happy with that, and we didn’t know that was going to take place, but it took place very quickly and it’s a magnificent deal for both.”
The Philippine president’s office later said both sides reached an understanding on areas of economic cooperation, but made no mention of a trade deal.
Trade representatives of both countries will work closely to translate the commitments into concrete initiatives, it said in a statement.
The deal with the Philippines would be great for US farmers and those in the energy business, Trump added on Truth Social, but gave no further details.
Negotiations on a trade deal between the two allies were not mentioned in any schedules released by either country.
There was no immediate comment from the office of Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr about the deal Trump was referring to.
“The US offered for us to diversify our food supply and energy requirements,” said Jose Manuel Romualdez, the Philippines’ ambassador to the United States.
Asked whether anything was signed, Romualdez said in a text message, “None.”
On Tuesday, Trump said Thailand would scrap all tariffs and substantial non-tariff barriers on its imports from the United States in a trade deal expected to be finalized in coming weeks.

Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Russia's energy crisis is so bad it's mass-importing fuel and looking to low-grade fuel for pump stations
articles.title_zh: Russia's energy crisis is so bad it's mass-importing fuel and looking to low-grade fuel for pump stations
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine's refinery strikes on Russia are pushing the world's second-biggest energy exporter to buy vast volumes of petrol from overseas and instruct officials to prioritize lower-quality fuel.
The crisis has been months in the making, as Kyiv wages a long-range strike campaign pummeling Russian energy facilities, claiming this week to have knocked out about 55% of total refinery capacity so far.
A new readout from a Russian government meeting on Tuesday signals how deep the Kremlin's fuel woes are growing.
Alexander Novak, a deputy prime minister and Russia's senior official overseeing energy, was cited telling his subordinates to prioritize expanding petrol imports and "securing additional volumes of out-of-class fuel."
The latter means that Moscow is now focusing on making lower-grade fuel available. It's traditionally held to a K5 rating, a quality standard its gas stations have maintained for 10 years.
Fuel below this rating was typically reserved for exports outside Russia's Eurasian trade bloc, as well as for niche uses such as the military, state reserves, or oilfields.
Meanwhile, local officials and media in at least six Russian regions announced gasoline rationing at some pump stations earlier this month, typically capping customers at 30 liters of petrol, or about 7.93 gallons, a day.
Reuters reported in August that similar restrictions had rolled out in Moscow areas among some chains, depending on the station type, with long queues forming outside some pumps near the capital.
Russia remains a net fuel exporter , shipping millions of tons of crude oil and other products like diesel abroad.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
But with its refineries under siege, it's struggled to turn enough of that crude into refined petrol for gas stations at home.
International organizations that track fuel shipments say Moscow has surged imports for those products over the last few months, mostly from Morocco, India, and Turkey.
While Russia's monthly fuel imports roughly maxed out at 5,000 metric tons of petrol products and additives from 2023 to 2025, it brought in over 416,000 metric tons of such goods by sea this August, according to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air.
The Helsinki-based non-profit said Russia further imported another 234,000 metric tons of seaborne oil products in September.
London-based shipping analytics firm Vortexa separately put Russia's August fuel imports at about 470,000 metric tons.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's military intelligence agency, GUR, said on Tuesday that Kyiv's attacks had forced Russia to import about 989,000 metric tons of fuel and high-octane additives by sea from July 18 to October 23.
Russia has also been importing fuel by rail, from countries like Belarus or Kazakhstan, though these aren't tracked as closely.
Reuters reported in July that Russia had imported about 453,000 metric tons in the first six months of 2026 over land, or about a 20-fold increase year-on-year.
The most recent time Russia shipped in fuel on those levels was in 2014, when it imported 1.6 million metric tons of motor gasoline amid a domestic supply squeeze.
Moscow had arranged a deal with Belarus to trade Russian crude oil for refined petrol it had previously sold to Minsk. The arrangement brought in another 808,000 metric tons in 2015.
But those imports took place over entire years, while GUR's estimate of nearly 1 million metric tons in imports covers just four months.
Novak, the senior Russian energy official, said in October that Russia was importing about 10% of its gasoline, though he did not provide any specific trade figures.
"We'll be importing at least until the end of the year," Novak told state media, adding that Russia also had to top up reserves depleted during the summer when gas ran short.
Novak's office and the Russian energy ministry did not immediately respond to comment requests sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider.

articles.title_orig: China’s Xi pitches free trade at APEC amid Trump’s global trade disruptions
articles.title_zh: China’s Xi pitches free trade at APEC amid Trump’s global trade disruptions
articles.content_orig:
China’s President Xi Jinping has urged support for “free and open trade”, pitching Beijing as a stable partner – as opposed to President Donald Trump-led Washington – and pledging to stand up to trade protectionism.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit on Wednesday in Shenzhen, southern China, Xi took aim at rising “unilateralism and protectionism”.
His remarks appeared to be a veiled criticism of Trump’s America First policies, under which the United States has imposed tariffs on both allies and economic rivals.
Xi is due to meet Trump, who is travelling from the Philippines for the APEC leaders’ summit later on Wednesday. Xi and Trump are then due to hold an unprecedented three-way summit with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
On the sidelines of the APEC summit, Xi told business executives that the Asia Pacific must pursue more open trade and equitable growth to remain stable and dynamic.
Trump’s America First approach of tariff hikes and other moves runs counter to APEC’s aim of eventually forming a Pacific Rim free trade zone.
Washington also limits Chinese access to leading-edge US technology, such as the Nvidia computer chips that help power artificial intelligence (AI).
“We must firmly uphold the rules-based multilateral trading system with the World Trade Organization at its core, support free and open trade and investment, maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial and supply chains,” Xi said.
He added that China sought to “provide a more stable, predictable and beneficial environment for global enterprises” and would continue to expand access in its manufacturing and services sectors.
“Starting by lowering tariffs, expanding access, and exploring regulations and management standards, China will conduct deep-seated reform,” Xi said.
“While pursuing its own development, China has shared opportunities with other countries and worked for common development,” he said. “It has steadily brought stability and predictability to world economic growth and international trade and economic cooperation.”
George Chen, partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, told the Associated Press news agency that Xi’s speech highlighted China’s aim to lead global industrial transformation.
“While he didn’t say so explicitly, his message was clear: China wants to be seen as a partner in global technology development, in contrast to Washington’s more restrictive approach,” Chen said, noting that Xi did not mention export controls, Nvidia, or the US directly.
Xi’s message is “likely to resonate with many Global South countries, and reinforces Beijing’s effort to contrast its technology strategy with that of Washington”, Chen added.

articles.title_orig: Record diesel prices drive UK inflation to 1-year high of 3.6%
articles.title_zh: Record diesel prices drive UK inflation to 1-year high of 3.6%
articles.content_orig:
U.K. inflation rose to 3.6% in the 12 months to October, its highest level in a year, as fuel costs continued to rise.
The reading was in line with the expectations of economists polled by Reuters and marked an increase from September's print of 3.5%.
October's reading puts U.K. inflation at a one-year high.
Britain's Office for National Statistics said the largest contributor to the rising inflation rate was motor fuel costs, which rose 33.2% year-on-year. It was the largest one-year rise in motor fuel prices since July 2022, when energy costs surged in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The U.K. is a net energy importer, making it vulnerable to external energy shocks such as the one sparked by the disruption of trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Oil prices have retreated from their wartime highs of well above $100 a barrel, but remain elevated.
The ONS said Wednesday that the average price of petrol rose by 5.2 pence (7 cents) per liter between September and October this year, compared with a 0.7 pence per liter rise in the same period a year earlier. The average petrol price stood at 174.7 pence per liter in October, the highest it's been since Aug. 2022.
Diesel prices rose by 7 pence per liter in October, with the average price reaching 199.5 pence per liter — the highest since ONS records began in 1996.
The Iran war has seen energy costs surge in various major economies. U.S. diesel prices hit $6 per gallon for the first time ever in September.
Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, inflation has risen sharply after a brief dip thanks to an energy price cap that was revised upward in July.
Earlier this month, the Bank of England hiked interest rates for the first time in three years, warning that inflation could hit 5% by mid-2027.
Governor Andrew Bailey said in the bank's November Monetary Policy Report that without "real progress towards settling the conflict in the Middle East... risks to energy prices, and so to inflation, are to the upside."
Markets are currently pricing in around an 80% chance of a rate hike at the Bank of England's final meeting of the year.
Scott Gardner, investment strategist at JPMorgan Personal Investing, said in a note following the release that a recent climb down in oil prices following the U.S. midterm elections could offer some relief in future inflation readings.
But he added: "While this may be a short-term reprieve for motorists, the broader outlook for UK inflation remains challenging as we approach 2027. After hiking interest rates at the start of the month, the Bank will be wary of a sustained uptick in inflation that could be here to stay."

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Framework announced its Wireless Touchpad Keyboard earlier this year with the goal of delivering a better couch keyboarding experience than the Logitech K400 . According to The Verge ’s Sean Hollister who went hands-on with Framework’s new all-in-one keyboard and touchpad last April, the company has succeeded in that goal, but it turns out you’ll be paying a bit more for Framework’s than Logitech’s.
While the K400 couch keyboard is $35, the Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is $99 with a $50 fully refundable deposit required to preorder one starting today . That makes it nearly three times more expensive than Logitech’s, but Framework’s upgrades and improvements could make it worth the premium.
Instead of starting from scratch, Framework uses the same keyboard module found in its Laptop 12 paired with a precision 120Hz touchpad and controller that’s also used in all of the company’s computers. A Bluetooth connection is the easiest way to pair the keyboard to PCs running Windows, Linux, or macOS, or mobile devices, game consoles, and streaming boxes. You can quickly switch between four wirelessly connected devices with a button press including one that uses an included USB receiver. If you want more responsiveness, you can also tether it to a device with a USB-C cable.
On a full charge of its replaceable 1,200mAh battery the keyboard will run for well over a year with sporadic use. If you’re instead using it for hours every day on a desk, Framework estimates the battery life will be closer to over a month. For customizability and remapping the keyboard’s open source firmware is based on a fork of ZMK .

articles.title_orig: Xi calls for greater Asia-Pacific trade openness ahead of Trump’s China visit (FXI:NYSEARCA)
articles.title_zh: Xi calls for greater Asia-Pacific trade openness ahead of Trump’s China visit (FXI:NYSEARCA)
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — Chinese President Xi Jinping opened a key Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting on Wednesday with calls for removing trade and investment barriers.
The leader spoke as he was expected to host Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump this week alongside the APEC CEO and Economic Leaders Summit.
"We should remove trade and investment barriers," Xi said via an official English translation. He said a key reason for doing so was "to promote development that is balanced."
He did not mention U.S. tariffs or other specific measures. Instead, Xi cast China as a "promising land for development" for global businesses, and indicated plans for "Bay Area" cooperation.
Shenzhen, home to major Chinese tech companies, is part of China's "Greater Bay Area" that includes Hong Kong and Macau. The Silicon Valley region around San Francisco is also known as the "Bay Area" in the U.S.
"China will not only cut tariffs and expand market access, but also go a step further," Xi said. He said China would "reform" rules and regulations to give foreign businesses "full manufacturing access."
Chinese exports have steadily grown their share of global manufactured goods, drawing criticism from the European Union and other regions for overcapacity. The U.S. and China last year agreed to keep tariffs lower, but the world's two largest economies have yet to implement a planned $30 billion cut in duties on goods from each side.
"Global growth lacks momentum," Xi noted in his speech. But he said "still global trade keeps growing against headwinds, and breakthroughs are being made in emerging technologies at a faster pace."
He said the "hard questions of our times" for Asia Pacific economies is whether to open, or close, doors — and later cast opening doors as bringing "progress."
"There can be no stability without security, and no security without stability," he said.
Xi called for APEC members to deepen coordination in the digital economy and AI, as a way to drive regional economic growth.
"Unicorn companies and large AI models have emerged in large numbers and many innovations have empowered hundreds of trades and industries and reached millions of households," he said, in some of his most specific mentions of the cutting-edge technology.

articles.title_zh: Target is set to report earnings before the bell. Here's what to expect
articles.content_orig:
Target is expected to report fiscal third-quarter results on Wednesday and offer more details on the progress of its turnaround as the company prepares for the busy holiday season.
The big-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. Last quarter, Target hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and said it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.
It's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high.
Here's what Wall Street is expecting for the retailer's fiscal third quarter, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Despite the progress, CEO Michael Fiddelke has emphasized that the company remains cautious about its turnaround, saying after Target's second-quarter results that the retailer has "much more work to do." While categories like food and beauty saw encouraging sales trends, the apparel and home categories lagged during that quarter.
Some investors still aren't sure Target has done enough to show a steady turnaround. Analysts at Morgan Stanley wrote in a note last week that they expect Target to deliver an "encouraging" quarter, though questions about the broader health of the business remain.
"Target has an opportunity to demonstrate progress, but the durability and profitability of its recovery remain open questions," the analysts wrote.
Still, they said they believe the company's investments in the store experience are driving interest from consumers.
Target's stock is up more than 60% this year.

articles.title_orig: China's Xi calls for upholding postwar international order at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen
articles.title_zh: China's Xi calls for upholding postwar international order at APEC CEO Summit in Shenzhen
articles.content_orig:
Host city offers showcase of China’s rise into a confident and innovative power central to global economy
I n a Shenzhen square on a balmy evening, locals and tourists watched the dozens of glinting towers that make up the city’s skyline ripple through the colour spectrum – cyan and violet, cyber green, China’s national scarlet and gold – repeatedly flashing the words “Apec 2026”.
The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit is a dream showcase for one of China’s most advanced cities, and the country’s leader, Xi Jinping , is basking in its neon glow.
On the sidelines, a series of high-profile bilateral meetings and the announcement of a historic three-way summit with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have cemented Xi’s status as an agenda setter on the global stage.
The broader Apec summit , meanwhile, provides an opportunity for China to present itself as a steward of multilateralism against what it terms “unilateralism and protectionism” – that is to say, trade measures taken against Beijing by countries such as the US.
All this is set against the futuristic backdrop that is Shenzhen, a city that perhaps better than no other embodies China’s rise into a confident, technologically innovative power central to the global economy.
A photo display in the Apec media centre charts Shenzhen’s transformation from sparsely populated marshland, calling it “a miracle in the history of world development created by the Chinese people”.
“[Xi] wants people to go home Chinamaxxing,” said Prof Astrid Nordin, of King’s College London. “Shenzhen is itself part of the message. It’s a showcase of Chinese technological and economic achievements, and of China’s claim that it offers opportunities for prosperity in a world increasingly characterised by uncertainty and conflict.”
Like the light show, the summit is being carefully coordinated. The Financial Times cited people familiar with the matter as saying it would be one of the most tightly controlled in the organisation’s history, with leaders having to travel to a state guesthouse beside Shenzhen’s tiger safari park to meet Xi. The paper said diplomats had grumbled that the format “seems designed to reduce the free-flowing discussion characteristic of prior editions”.
Setting out its expectations for the summit, China’s foreign ministry has said it looks forward to “practical results in key areas such as trade, connectivity, digital economy, AI and so on”.
Already, Xi has announced trade wins with Canada’s Mark Carney, extending remission measures for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products by two years in exchange for tariff relief on Canadian pork, fish and seafood exports.
A meeting with Papua New ⁠Guinea’s leader, meanwhile, showed how Beijing’s geopolitical priorities have been absorbed and reflected by its allies, with James Marape recounting to Xi how he had closed Taiwan’s office in his country despite domestic challenges in doing so.
The most important meeting will be between Xi and Trump. The leaders of the world’s two superpowers are expected to tackle a broad range of issues including AI and trade. In a move that could strain the fragile tariff truce that the two leaders first agreed last year, the Trump administration said on Monday it would further restrict China’s access to advanced AI chips.
Christopher Adams, a senior adviser at the law firm Covington who was at the centre of trade negotiations with China for the Obama and first Trump administrations, said: “The trade truce may increasingly look like a ceasefire in a war where major combat operations remain on hold but skirmishes are escalating to the point where the line between peace and war is blurred.
“I don’t see pressure to announce a further extension of the trade truce in Shenzhen. If a significant extension is announced, that would be an upside surprise.”
China has not hesitated to leverage Apec’s multinational platform in service of its arguments. A commentary by the state news agency Xinhua on Tuesday said: “Amid deepening geopolitical rivalries and growing global divisions, [China’s hosting] sends a clear signal that great-power competition need not be a zero-sum game, and that one country’s development need not come at the expense of another.”
The chair of the Apec senior officials’ meeting, Chen Xu, said Beijing had made trade “openness” a key focus of its Apec year and looked forward to “achieving more practical outcomes on the trade front”.
The much anticipated trilateral summit with Trump and Putin, on the other hand, could prove largely symbolic. For Xi, “it provides the appearance of China shaping the world order as an equal to the United States,” said Dr Kevork Oskanian, an expert on Russia at the University of Exeter. “Agreement on substantial issues, which would, in any case, require extensive preparatory negotiations, is unlikely.”
For China’s ruling Communist party, the political pomp has another key purpose. Nordin said summits were “occasions for leaders to tell stories about the world, about their country’s place in it … and one of the most important audiences for those stories is at home.”
For the locals watching the skyscraper light show on Monday night, the symbolism was not lost. China’s export might had helped it become increasingly powerful on the world stage, said one local man, who did not give his name. “It’s so great that the summit will take place in Shenzhen,” he said. “I feel very proud.”

articles.title_orig: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
articles.title_zh: With Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AI
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.title_orig: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
articles.title_zh: Rare images of Indigenous group in Amazon highlight threats, advocates say
articles.content_orig:
Rare images of an isolated Indigenous group emerging from a remote part of Brazil’s Amazon rainforest have highlighted the threats they face from loggers, hunters and ranchers, advocates say.
Survival International, a UK-based Indigenous rights group, shared images on Tuesday of a “historic encounter” on Monday in the northeastern state of Maranhao between a government team and about 20 uncontacted Awa people, who asked for food.
The Awa are a Tupi-Guarani people in northwestern Maranhao, some of whom remain in voluntary isolation, according to Funai, Brazil’s Indigenous affairs agency.
Funai told the Reuters news agency it was reviewing videos and accounts on social media showing isolated Awa interacting with a village in the Arariboia Indigenous Land, and that the Brazilian state was not seeking contact with the group, in line with its policy of non-contact.
Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples said the encounter began on Monday near a government access control post and the village of Tawari, home to Guajajara Indigenous people, The Associated Press (AP) news agency reported. The footage was recorded by members of the Guajajara community, according to AP.
Survival International said it released the footage at the request of the Guardians of the Amazon, an Indigenous group that campaigns against illegal loggers and ranchers.
“The uncontacted Awa are under extreme pressure as intruders encroach from all sides of their territory, driving them into an ever-smaller island of the Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” said Caroline Pearce, Survival International’s director.
The Maranhao Indigenous people’s organisation COAPIMA said the encounter showed the need for careful action by the responsible agencies because of the risks that unplanned contact can pose to isolated groups , mainly from exposure to diseases.
In recent decades, isolated Indigenous groups across the Amazon have faced encroaching illegal miners, loggers and ranchers.
Contact with the groups can be deadly. In Colombia, about 40 percent of the isolated Nukak people died from diseases after outsiders reached them in the 1980s.
“If there is no forest, there are no uncontacted peoples,” Teresa Mayo, a senior researcher at Survival International, told Al Jazeera in a report on the Nukak.

articles.title_orig: Beijing: China, Canada agree to 2-year extension of exemptions
articles.title_zh: Beijing: China, Canada agree to 2-year extension of exemptions
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING – China and Canada have agreed to extend relevant exemption measures under a preliminary joint arrangement on bilateral trade issues by two years, China's Ministry of Commerce said on Tuesday.
Canada will further expand exemptions for Chinese steel and aluminum products, while China will adjust anti-discrimination measures on certain Canadian agricultural and aquatic products in accordance with relevant laws and regulations, a ministry spokesperson said in response to a media query.
ALSO READ: China expands export control on precursor chemicals to US, Mexico, Canada
Guided by the important consensus reached between the leaders of the two countries, China and Canada have held multiple rounds of economic and trade consultations in the spirit of mutual respect and win-win cooperation, reaching a supplementary joint arrangement on trade issues of mutual concern, the spokesperson said.
The two sides also reached positive consensus on economic and trade issues, including e-commerce cooperation, the establishment of branches of Chinese-funded banks in Canada, and improvements to the business environment, according to the spokesperson.
READ MORE: Commerce ministry: China willing to lengthen cooperation list with Canada
The spokesperson expressed confidence that these arrangements will help deepen bilateral economic and trade cooperation and bring greater benefits to the people of both countries.
Both sides will expedite their respective domestic procedures to put the agreed measures into effect as soon as possible and continue exploring further arrangements to deepen economic and trade cooperation, the spokesperson said.
READ MORE: China and Canada agree to address EV, rapeseed issues
The spokesperson added that the two countries will make full use of the China-Canada Joint Economic and Trade Commission mechanism to expand cooperation, resolve problems, manage differences and promote the sound, stable and sustainable development of bilateral economic and trade relations.
The preliminary joint arrangement between China and Canada was reached during Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's visit to China in January, covering trade issues including electric vehicles, steel and aluminum products, and agricultural and aquatic products.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Earnings Live Updates: First Report Since Jensen Huang’s Resignation Beats Expectations
articles.content_orig:
The fallout from Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy as well as an Nvidia executive that led to his resignation as CEO of Nivida , the company he founded and grew into a $4 trillion chip giant, will likely go on for some time.
But the missteps of Nvidia's board of directors offer immediate lessons, say talent and leadership experts. It shows what happens when there's no clear succession plan, the dangers of an overly decentralized leadership structure, and how companies built around one powerful, controlling leader create the kind of risk boards are responsible for preventing.
In the span of less than a week — from the time Huang admitted that he was unfaithful to his wife until the board announced that he was resigning — the question became: could Nvidia, a company at the epicenter of the AI build-out, operate without him?
With Huang's ouster and the appointment of CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO , Nvidia's employees, customers, and investors will begin to find out. The process will also put a glaring spotlight on why the Nvidia board wasn't better prepared for Huang leaving the company for whatever reason.
"Succession planning is an ongoing, fundamental responsibility of the board, not something to do when a crisis hits," says Lisa Calicchio, chief human resources officer at WCG Clinical and a member of the CNBC Workforce Executive Council .
She described what happened at Nvidia as "a failure of epic proportion, both on the part of the board for not fulfilling its fiduciary responsibility to ensure continued viability of the organization by having a robust succession plan, and for the behavior and risks created by the CEO."
"What they're doing now is flying by the seat of their pants," she added.
Nvidia's 10-member board of directors is a collection of early investors, long-time partners and business executives across a range of industries. Before Nov. 12, the company did not have a chair of the board or any clear succession plan . The board also includes directors who expressed "confidence in Jensen" before they had even begun their own independent internal review of his actions.
In addition to naming Kress to the top job, the company appointed Harvey C. Jones, a tech investor and Nvidia director for the past 33 years, as its first-ever chair. After his appointment, the company announced that the board would be conducting a search of both internal and external candidates to find a permanent chief executive.
Alan Fleischmann, founder and CEO of business advisory firm Laurel Strategies and a member of the CNBC CEO Council , says that while "the DNA of any organization is defined by the CEO, there must be a stronger board dynamic and strong leadership surrounding the CEO."
"Succession planning is not simply about identifying who takes over when a CEO leaves," Fleischmann said. "It's about building an institution that can thrive beyond any one individual."
The outsized role Huang played at Nvidia — in September 2025 he told CNBC's Becky Quick that he had as many as 60 direct reports — makes it even more difficult for the board to find someone who can understand the inner workings of the company while being such a visible and active hype man for its all-important AI chips.
In corporate governance circles this is known as "key man" risk and it points to a company being overly reliant on one person whose death, departure, or financial or moral compromise could materially damage the organization.
"This is the world's most valuable company and all the risk centered on the shoulders of one man," Calicchio says.
"Flat organizations can be remarkably effective…but there are tradeoffs," Fleischmann added. "When too many decisions, relationships and reporting lines converge around one individual, the organization can become more vulnerable than it appears."
Calicchio acknowledged that a CEO having numerous direct reports isn't problematic in the early days of a company, when the founder knows everyone, but becomes concerning "when a company is the size of Nvidia. I really question the rigor and discipline of their organizational policies."
This same absence of rigor is evident in the lack of any obvious successors to Huang. "You would expect the board to have recognized at some point there was going to be an increasing need to look beyond Jensen," says Tim Wentworth, the former CEO of Walgreens Boots Alliance and Express Scripts. "This sounds so fundamental, but you don't wait for the rainy day to have the rainy day plan."
Wentworth says that when he was running both Walgreens and Express Scripts, he had a single board member assigned to each one of his direct reports so that "when we had board discussions, somebody in the room could speak about them and their strengths."
At WCG Clinical, succession and talent discussions are done quarterly, says Calicchio. "We're always looking at time frames," she says. "Is this person a definite successor, ready now, or is this someone you're grooming for the long term? Everyone wants to think that replacing the CEO is going to happen in an orderly way, but as we just saw at Nvidia, that's not always the case."
"Boards need to expect the unexpected," she adds.
Huang's powerful grip at Nvidia was great, "until it wasn't," says Wentworth. "It's really hard for a board to have a sense of urgency and the depth of intrusiveness necessary in that process when everything is going great with the company. No one wants to be the contrarian, but that's your job as a board member."
To join the CNBC Workforce Executive Council, apply at cnbccouncils.com/wec .

articles.title_zh: Xiaomi 18 purportedly leaks in live image - GSMArena.com news
articles.content_orig:
Xiaomi took the Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max global at an event in Paris today , and it seems like the vanilla Xiaomi 18 wants a bit of the spotlight too. A tipster on X has shared what's purportedly the first live image of the phone, which you can see below.
The white unit in the photo has a metal frame and a squircle camera island with three cameras. Unlike its Pro siblings, however, there's no secondary display on the back.
The tipster also shared the phone's expected specs, which mostly (but not entirely) line up with what leaked back in September . The Xiaomi 18 is said to have a flat 6.4-inch "1.5K" 120Hz LTPO OLED with TCL's M11 panel, the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chipset, a 200MP main camera with OIS, a 50MP ultrawide, and a 50MP telephoto with OIS, along with a battery of around 7,000 mAh with 100W wired charging. It's also tipped to come with an IP69 rating, an ultrasonic fingerprint scanner, and a USB 3.2 port.
That telephoto is a bit of a departure from the September leak, which claimed the Xiaomi 18 would get a 200MP periscope with 3x optical zoom, just like the Pro models. The battery was also tipped at 7,200 mAh back then. The phone is expected to launch in China in December, so we should know for sure soon enough.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
articles.title_zh: Nvidia's Colette Kress tells Cramer: Employees and customers are not going anywhere
articles.content_orig:
AI investors and beyond were eagerly anticipating Nvidia's ( NVDA -0.44% ) earnings call Tuesday night. The earnings report was the company's first since Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO amid controversy last week. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as the interim CEO as it conducts a search for a permanent replacement, considering both internal and external candidates.
Kress passed her first test with flying colors, as she delivered a confident pitch for the company and even raised guidance for fiscal 2028 from 70% revenue growth to 75% revenue growth. Nvidia also beat estimates on the top and bottom lines, and the stock was trading higher after the call, up 3.3% as of 8:23 p.m.
However, amid the focus on the headline numbers and parsing the call for hints into the company's future, there was one key comment from Kress that investors may have missed.
It's understandable why Nvidia is down a third from its peak last month, given Huang's sudden exit, but with Nvidia stock now trading at a forward P/E of just 11, the stock is as cheap as it's ever been and ripe for share buybacks.
In response to a question about the company's capital allocation and its buyback plans, Kress said that the "super top priority" for returning capital to shareholders was to use the company's current share repurchase authorization, which was raised by $150 billion in September and sat at $227.3 billion at the end of the third quarter. Kress added, "So thinking about all of that together, I think there is definitely room to continue all of the stock repurchase plans that we want to do and complete those before the end of fiscal year '28." She also noted that the top priority for its capital spending is supporting its suppliers in building out additional capacity.
If Nvidia executes on those buybacks and the stock price stays roughly the same, it would reduce shares outstanding by roughly 6% by Jan. 2028, when fiscal 2028 ends.
The share repurchase authorization and Kress's commitment are a positive sign, not just because it will lift Nvidia's earnings per share, but because it shows management's confidence that the stock is undervalued after the recent sell-off and signals to investors that it's worth buying.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/17/26
For investors worried that Nvidia would struggle during the transitional period, Kress gave no indication that anything has changed, saying, "it's business as usual," and that customers, suppliers, and partners are all "100% behind us."
Demand for the company's products continues to outstrip supply, and Kress spent much of the call reiterating the company's commitment to securing adequate supply, which allowed it to raise its revenue guidance for fiscal 2028.
In just one quarter, its supply commitments increased from $279 billion, primarily due to memory supply. Kress said, "We feel confident in terms of both the demand that we have in front of us as well as the supply and additionally that we can do the 75%," referring to 75% revenue growth next year.
Nvidia also addressed the controversy around Jensen Huang, and new Chairman of the Board Harvey Jones made it clear that the board has no intention of reinstating Huang. Regarding the CEO search, Jones said, "We want to install this CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person." Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, who has been seen as a possible replacement for Huang, was on the Q&A portion of the call, but did not answer any questions.
Nvidia did what it needed to do on the earnings call and then some. Its commitment to using up its $227 billion share repurchase authorization and the guidance hike for fiscal 2028 show investors the company continues to excel. Nvidia is on track to bring in more than $700 billion in revenue next year. Given the deep discount, Nvidia looks like a buy , even without Jensen Huang.

articles.title_orig: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages
articles.title_zh: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages
articles.content_orig:
Chief Correspondent covering media and technology
Did AI cause the US government to shut down all air travel Friday?
Could be, says the US government.
Also, maybe not. Who knows? But don't worry.
That's the confusing answer from Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. He went on Fox News on Monday and said that the nationwide grounding last week — as well as other recent high-profile outages at places like JPMorgan, Microsoft , and United — might have all stemmed from organizations introducing new AI software into their IT stacks.
Why does he think that? Because "one guy that's very smart with tech," — not Elon Musk, Mullin specified — told him that. And "that kinda makes sense to me."
I mean, it also kinda makes sense to me? Maybe? But I'm not running a federal agency with more than 200,000 workers and an annual budget of more than $100 billion.
But Mullin said he really doesn't know. He does know that "we just have a lot of technologists [sic] thrown at us and our world runs on technology now. We used to have backup systems. And the backup systems are overwhelmed by the new systems now."
Then Mullin told Fox viewers that they should "breathe." And be assured that the US is probably not under a cyber attack — something he felt "98%" confident about.
I would very much like to live in a world where a top federal official doesn't muddle through national news interviews about outages. I would very much like to live in a world where the administration hadn't spent much of last year telling us the federal government was incompetent and should be radically downsized . Because sometimes we really want the federal government — not "one guy" — to be able to tell us what's actually happening inside these complicated systems, and what should be done about it.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
But I also think we'd have these exact same problems if we had the most competent, well-meaning public servants in charge right now.
That's because all of this stuff is gnarly and complicated. Long before the AI boom, we've had technologists pointing out how rickety and poorly maintained much of America's digital and physical infrastructure is — and how seemingly isolated problems can have enormous ripple effects. Perhaps you recall the giant blackout of 2003 , where big swaths of the country, including New York City, lost power because of a software glitch in Ohio.
Now we've added AI to the mix —a technology so new and head-scratching that the people who are building it frequently say they're not really sure how it works , and aren't exactly sure how to control it .
Which is why people who have talked to more than "one guy" often tell us to buckle up for more instability. "We should plan to wake up in Software Beirut, where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time," as journalist Josh Tyrangiel put it in The Atlantic .
What can you, a normal person, do about this? Here I agree with Markwayne Mullin: You shouldn't do anything. There's nothing much you can do, aside from the digital equivalent of making sure you have some soup cans and water bottles handy, just in case.
But if you're a member of the media — that is, anyone with access to a keyboard and an internet connection — things get a little trickier. It is reasonable to cover all of these outages, ask why they're happening, and not accept the hand-wavy answers you often get right after an event. But also be ready to accept that sometimes things break because things break, and that sometimes a coincidence is a coincidence. Or that maybe it's all a squirrel's fault .
That's not an easy balance to pull off. Ring the bell every time there's a possible threat, and you'll end up with a country that's permanently on edge — or worse, doesn't pay attention to any warnings at all. Wait too long before ringing the bell, and people may be woefully unprepared. It's a real challenge .
That said, one very easy step is to just stay mute when you don't have anything helpful to say.
Tuesday morning, I got asked to come on an interview show to discuss "the November 17 blackout," which confused me since I was unaware there had been a blackout Tuesday.
Turns out it was a reference to a made-up thing on social media , and I'm not going to spend more time discussing a non-thing here.
Except to say that it's one thing for your uncle to pass along a hoax email to his friends and family. And it's another to go on TV or the internet and give the hoax that much more oxygen. Even if you're ostensibly going to debunk the hoax, you're still spreading the particulates around.
But Markwayne Mullin? I'd definitely like you to ask a few more people — perhaps there are still technology experts in your organization, for starters — for more information. Then come back and tell us what you've learned. We'd love to know more.
